CLARIFICATION OF TERMS:

There are some concepts for which we don't really have names right now. As our knowledge of AI expands, there will be more and more words that are added that don't exist right now.

For example "grokking" is now used to describe when a neural nets rapidly learns a skill after a period of not having any visible progress. (the word appeared in an excellent sci fi book a long time ago, but only recently used in ML)

In this video, I use a lot of words that are best approximations for these terms.

For example I say the model can "visualize" or "see" the board. It's unlikely that there are actual visuals as we understand them. The point is that it can understand the board and where the pieces are and if each square is empty or has a tile.

It also probably doesn't understand what "square" or "tile" actually are, just some representation of those concepts that it understands.

So, a lot of these words I use here, are not to be taken literally. They are just some words that we would use to describe a human equivalent. Likely all these terms will be added over time as we learn more.

What convinced me that there definitely is some kind of understanding of concepts embedded in the model was one test I did with it.

I created a program in a fictional programming language that I made up on the spot. It was gibberish, but I tried to make it logical enough so that a programmer could understand the different functions if I told them what the goal of the program was. It represented a simple 6 sided dice roller. I then gave Bing (GPT-4) the program and told it it was a dice roller, nothing more. Then I asked it to modify the program so it would roll a 12 sided die 6 times. And lo and behold, it made the changes that I would've made. I also asked it to explain the different functions and it mostly understood it the way I intended it. The program was very short and simple, but I was amazed. In my view, this would have been impossible if it was just a stochastic parrot. I think this test absolutely requires some kind of intelligence.

In my somewhat limited understanding of the topic the primary difference has been explained to me to be about parallelism. Each single neuron in your brain can have thousands of other neurons connected to it. When a neuron fires the "weights" are automatically calculated as it's based on the strength of the connection between the neurons and the signal is propagated out as neural activations creating a continuous cascade which all occur in parallel simultaneously.
Meanwhile each layer in a LLM has billions of weighted parameters, then the cpu/gpu calculates all these weights of the active layer and passes it on to the next layer, this happens 96 times for something like GPT3 but once a layer has calculated it's weights it no longer continues in parallelism with the other layers or activates recursively, its (basically) just a linear pass through.
AI could certainly become intelligent(or maybe already is), but so long as we use this type of architecture that doesn't emphasize parallelism like our brains do it's going to foster a different and unfamiliar kind of intelligence to how we traditionally assess something as "intelligent".
Which is kind of what we see, a LLM can't have "branching" thoughts like people do, and when not prompted with an input for it's layers to resolve it's entirely void of any "thought" or calculations, unlike with a human our neurons are constantly firing and it takes us considerable effort and meditation to slow down and "clear" our minds even by a small amount. We are almost always thinking and never void of thought, even in our sleep.

I probably missed something, but the paper doesn't seem very compelling.
The sequence of letters and numbers is itself a representation of whether any cell corresponding to any letter and number is empty or not. If you train the model with millions of examples, the latent space will expand to consider all the cells in the board.
So then if you use a different model (the probe) to predict, based on the state of the weights of the first model, whether a certain cell in the board is filled or not, it will be able to do so, because the first model has all the information it needs for a different model to predict that.
This doesn't mean, to my perspective, that the first model created a full "world model", but just that its status contains all the information needed to infer the state of the model, which is what I would expect anyways.

In any case, even if it's true that LLMs create world models (and I believe it is regardless of this paper), that doesn't prove that they have "understanding", if we use the intuitive definition of this word. 
It does only prove that they are intelligent and that they are following a statistical inferred model of the world, but not that they posses a conscious understanding of it. 

When people and philosohers talk about "understanding", they intuitively imply a conscious awareness that something is true. 
If I claim that I understand the layout of a chess board, I mean that I have a conscious perception of how the chess board looks like, what is its purpose, its meaning, why it's constructed in this way and not in a different way and so.
The semantic awareness, the subjective conscious perception of the meaning is always implied.

A machine doesn't have that. A machine goes through the motions based on instructions, it's just opened or closed electron gates in a silicon board. There is no subjective perception or awareness of anything, as there doesn't need to be in order to simulate reasoning.
If you simulate a galaxy in a computer, to any level of degree, even at the Planck scale, it won't actually create gravity. In the same way, a simulation of a brain won't actually create consciousness.

We have abstracted the discussion in Computer Science so much that very intelligent people are unable to see this obvious fact.

If you're still on the fence and you think LLMs are conscious, I'd suggest you to please look into Federico Faggin (inventor of the first commercial microprocessor), Donal Hoffman (Computer Scientist, Neurologist and Mathematician) and Bernardo Kastrup (Philosoher, Computer Scientist and Physicist who worked at CERN).

AI And The New Luddites
In the age of innovation, I, an enlightened Luddite, stand not against technology itself, but against the capricious embrace of that which functions erratically or displays madness. As we navigate this modern world, let us discern the virtuous from the vexatious among our technological marvels.

True marvels
Consider the marvels of modernity: planes that carry us to distant realms, cars that whisk us across lands, computers that tether our thoughts to an intangible web, and yes, even the Language and Learning Models (LLMs) that endeavor to understand our musings. These, my friends, are commendable if they adhere to the creed of functionality and sanity.
In the realm of innovation, should we not acknowledge the audacious creator of the LLM transformer? If the custodians of the Nobel Prize can christen it under the auspices of Economics or even Literature, who are we to protest? Yet, as I have oft maintained, my ire is directed at technology that strays into the domains of derangement.

Futile Innovation
Let us dissect the hallmarks of futile innovation, for the annals of history teem with examples. The creators of the Concord, seemed to not know that their creation tried to fly at speeds of 1400 miles per hour. The architects of the space shuttle, in a parallel feat of ignorance, failed to grasp that each launch hoisted a colossal 100,000-kilogram spacefaring leviathan. Apple, too, harbored its own befuddlements, as its designers—strangely ignorant—deemed it appropriate to bestow their beloved iFone with neither a battery nor an on/off switch.

Blind to mathematics - those AI geniuses
And then, the engineers and designers behind AI—a field that prides itself on intelligence—display baffling obliviousness. They appear blind to the mathematical edifice that underpins their endeavors,  the scaffold of factorial mathematics. 

The rigid wall
These architects seem ignorant of the inexorable wall presented by those factorial equations, when compared with the mere exponential gains in computer devices. This is an oversight akin to pitting a cheetah against an earthworm in a race of acceleration.

“There ain’t gonna be no ASI,” is the wisdom of new generation of Luddites, and its based on certainty, as surely as the number N! reaches near infinity.

The thing that beguiled impressionable hearts
Now, permit me to address the notorious iFone—a relic that beguiled the impressionable hearts of the youthful twenty-somethings. An artifact seemingly conceived with clarity of purpose, it could not solve a puzzle of its own making—an enigma that existed solely within its circuitry. Recall, if you will, the sagacious utterances of the late Steve Jobs, who, with prophetic insight, acknowledged the non-existence of the very quandary his creation sought to vanquish. Yet, with a twist that would humble even the most Machiavellian of minds, this device was artfully perverted into a mechanism to ensnare the unsuspecting masses.

The expletive-laden contraption
Today, the once-young disciples of this false idol find themselves in the throes of their mid-thirties, grappling with the existential lament: "Why, in the name of reason, do I persist in tolerating this expletive-laden contraption?" This, dear reader, is the lingering refrain of a generation ensnared by the siren call of deceitful innovation.

A discerning eye
In this grand theater of technology and its follies, let us not forget that our enlightenment lies not in an outright rejection of progress, but in a discerning eye cast upon its treacheries. For in the maelstrom of invention, it is the privilege and duty of the enlightened to champion the cause of sanity, and above all, the wisdom to recognize when the emperor's new clothes,  and maybe her large language models intended to be ASI, are naught but rags, stapled onto the rigid and unyielding walls of mathematics.
